title: Voynich Manuscript: What Carbon-14 Dating Revealed About the World's Most Mysterious Codex

content:
Yale MS 408 dated to 1404–1438 by the University of Arizona. How radiocarbon testing disproved modern forgery theories and why Turing and NSA failed to crack it.

• November 18, 2026

In 20 seconds: The Voynich Manuscript (cataloged as MS 408 at Yale University’s Beinecke Library) is a 240-page parchment codex written in an undeciphered script accompanied by fantastical botanical, astronomical, and anatomical drawings. In 2009, radiocarbon testing by the University of Arizona dated the vellum conclusively to between 1404 and 1438, definitively debunking modern forgery claims while leaving its linguistic meaning, author, and purpose completely unsolved.

  • Documented Provenance: Rediscovered in 1912 by Polish-American book dealer Wilfrid Voynich at the Jesuit College of Villa Mondragone in Frascati, Italy.
  • Scientific Vellum Dating: Accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) confirmed the calfskin parchment was created during the early 15th-century Renaissance.
  • Cryptanalytic Dead End: Neither William Friedman (chief cryptanalyst of the NSA's precursor), Alan Turing at Bletchley Park, nor modern neural networks have deciphered a single verifiable sentence.

What exactly is the Voynich Manuscript?

Cataloged under the designation MS 408, the manuscript is an octavo-sized codex measuring roughly 22.5 by 16 centimeters. It contains approximately 240 vellum folios, though lacunae in the historical numbering indicate that several leaves were lost before Wilfrid Voynich acquired it in 1912.

The entire text is penned in an unidentified cursive script featuring an alphabet of between 20 and 25 distinct glyphs. What makes the codex so mesmerizing—and frustrating for philologists—is its fluid, uniform execution: there are no crossed-out words, no hesitations, and no punctuation marks typical of scribal drafting.

The manuscript is conventionally divided into five thematic sections based on its illustrations:

  1. Herbal Section: Drawings of 113 unidentified plants, many appearing to be bizarre chimeras of roots, leaves, and petals from distinct botanical families.
  2. Astronomical & Astrological Section: Fold-out diagrams featuring celestial spheres, zodiac symbols, and circular diagrams with tiny female figures.
  3. Balneological Section: Complex plumbing networks and pools where unclothed female figures bathe in green liquids.
  4. Cosmological Section: Intricate circular rosettes, maps, and geometric foldouts.
  5. Pharmaceutical Section: Jars, containers, and roots accompanied by short labeling annotations.

The 2009 Carbon-14 Breakthrough

For decades, skeptics argued that the manuscript might be a clever 16th-century Elizabethan fraud concocted by alchemist Edward Kelley, or even a 20th-century counterfeit fabricated by Wilfrid Voynich himself using blank Renaissance parchment.

In 2009, a multidisciplinary research team led by physicist Dr. Greg Hodgins at the University of Arizona’s NSF-Arizona AMS Facility obtained permission to extract four micro-samples from different folios. Using accelerator mass spectrometry, the researchers dated the organic collagen of the parchment:

The calibrated radiocarbon analysis pinpointed the animal slaughter and vellum manufacture to between 1404 and 1438 AD. Subsequent chemical testing by the McCrone Research Institute in Chicago demonstrated that the iron-gall ink had seeped deeply into the vellum’s microscopic crevices during the period of manufacture, confirming that the writing was not added centuries later over aged parchment.

Why Codebreakers and AI Keep Failing

If the manuscript was written over 600 years ago in Central Europe, why has nobody been able to read it?

During World War II, William F. Friedman—the legendary cryptanalyst who broke Japan’s PURPLE cipher—formed a dedicated civilian study group to attack the text. Friedman discovered that Voynichese displays low entropy: words are unusually repetitive, and letters exhibit strict positional constraints (certain glyphs only appear at the beginning of words, others only at the end).

Furthermore, statistical analysis demonstrated that the manuscript obeys Zipf’s Law, a universal mathematical property of natural human languages where word frequency follows a strict logarithmic curve. Random gibberish or improvised hoaxes created in the 1400s do not exhibit Zipfian distributions.

Modern machine learning models and large language models (LLMs) have repeatedly attempted to map Voynichese onto Hebrew, Turkish, Latin, and proto-Romance dialects. In each case, the proposed translations rely on arbitrary anagramming or selective letter substitutions that collapse when applied consistently across all 240 folios.

Until a bilingual key or cryptographic Rosetta Stone is discovered, the Voynich Manuscript remains what Yale University calls it: the ultimate open book that nobody can read.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is the Voynich Manuscript kept today and can it be viewed online?

The original codex, cataloged as MS 408, is permanently housed in the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library at Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut. High-resolution digital scans of all 240 surviving folios are publicly accessible in Yale's digital collections.

What did the 2009 carbon-14 test prove about the Voynich Manuscript?

A team led by Dr. Greg Hodgins at the University of Arizona performed accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) radiocarbon dating on four parchment samples. The tests established with 95% statistical confidence that the vellum was produced between 1404 and 1438, ruling out theories that it was a 16th-century forgery by John Dee or a modern fabrication by Wilfrid Voynich.

Has anyone successfully deciphered the Voynich text?

No. Despite claims by academic and amateur cryptographers over the past century, there is no peer-reviewed consensus on any translation. Renowned cryptanalysts including William F. Friedman and Alan Turing failed to break the code, and recent automated translation claims have been widely refuted.

What is Zipf's Law and does the Voynich text obey it?

Zipf's Law states that in natural human languages, the frequency of any word is inversely proportional to its rank in the frequency table. Mathematical analyses confirm that 'Voynichese' adheres strictly to Zipf's Law, suggesting it is either a genuine unknown language or an extraordinarily sophisticated cipher constructed with linguistic properties.
